speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OP ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
There are one or two
other features of the minister's statement of yesterday to which I want to refer. The minister made some very favourable comments on the great success of the government in getting its new railway loans floated at a cheaper rate than those floated in 1919-20. I
know the minister well enough to assert with positiveness that he was quite aware that there was not the slightest thing in what he was contending; that it was merely a question of what the value of money was in the world's markets, and that the government were no more responsible for the money rate of 1924 than they were for the price of wheat in 1924; no more responsible than they were for the cattle values of 1922. What is possible in these matters is entirely a matter of market conditions, and if the minister intended to make an argument the only way he could have set about it was to compare the rates this company was able to secure on government guarantee with rates which other governments were able to secure in other parts of the world. Into this he did not launch; consequently I have not overstepped the mark when I say that his words were merely vain. Attempts have been made frequently to make these comparisons. They are very easily made. If hon. members will look at the Hansard report of the budget debate of 1923, and especially at certain accounts of loans presented by the former Minister of Finance, the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), they will get all the information they desire to show that the lowest possible interest rate was secured in 1920 and 1921, and that our bonds were sold on an interest basis lower than were those of any other country at the same time.
While I am on the subject I wish to say a word on a matter very much akin to it. Repeated assertions come rather flippantly, I think, from many members of the government and from some hon. members to my left, to the effect that a very stupid and a very gross financial crime was perpetuated when, during the war, tax-free bonds were issued. It is hard for me to conceive of anything more futile or more childish than the attempts of hon. members to declare how much has been lost to Canadla by the issue of these tax-free bonds. It would be just as easy to ascertain how much more rainfall we would have had in these ten years had there not been an earthquake in San Francisco. No man knows, or can know, or give an intelligent opinion, whether or not there has been a dollar lost to Canada. One would actually think that a decision to issue the bonds tax free was come to in order to see that people who had money to lend at that time would be in a comfortable position for the rest of their lives; that the treasury was not considered; that the tax-payer was not considered'-only the money lender. Well, I do not think any government or any party

C.NJt.-Minister's Statement
is so utterly idiotic as that, and I do not think any hon. member thinks it is; much less that the Minister of Finance of that time, whose record during the war will bear comparison with that of the Finance minister of any other allied country, would have been guilty of conduct so careless or precipitate. Every consideration was weighed on all sides of the argument. We were faced with this condition. The American republic was issuing tax-free bonds, and issued them throughout the war-has been issuing them right up to this day. And these people are referred to by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) as the shrewdest financiers in the world. I do not think he is very far astray; there are just as good, but there are no better. They believe it pays to do that; and the ascending scale of their income tax law is even more precipitate now than ours, for they have lowered their income tax on the lower incomes while those remaining at the high figure are unchanged. I quote one sentence from the annual report of the treasurer of the United States, issued just a few months ago:
Fully tax exempt securities outstanding in the hands of the public now amount to $13,284,000,000 and are increasing at the rate of one billion dollars a year.
This is the conduct of those men described by the minister as the shrewdest financiers in the world; but this conduct, or exactly the same conduct on our part is referred to by those super-financiers to my left and opposite me as the work of childish knaves. No; the money had to be secured; failure to secure it would have been fatal. Looking back upon the period now from the vantage ground of ten years thence, we may be honestly convinced that the money could have been secured if the bonds had not been tax free. One thing is certain: a higher price would have had to be paid. Whether that higher figure would in the long event have counterbalanced the taxes we now might collect; no man can say. But how is anyone to tell at the opening of a great war, or even a year after, or two, or three, what is to be the burden when the war is over, and what is to be the history of taxation for years thereafter? The best judgment, the judgment exercised by other nations at the same time, was exercised here, and the considerations that moved the financiers of other countries moved the Finance Minister of Canada. Certainly no one could honestly even think-no one could honestly say-that any other consideration affected him at all. Even to-day the United States of America adopt this plan of securing loans. Nobody would suggest that they could not secure them were the

bonds not tax free. Certainly they could; their country is abounding with money within all its boundaries. But their judgment is that in this way they can get the loan more cheaply and in the end be in a better position than if they issued them otherwise.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
Those are the circumstances to which I wished to refer, and I have taken the liberty of doing so notwithstanding the fact that it is aside from the main current of the minister's
statement.
The Minister of Railways then went into the question of the condition of the system and the results of last year, and expressed the view that the result was wholly satisfactory, and indeed phenomenally so under all the circumstances. Well, the qualifying phrase is, of course, a very useful one-a very sweeping one. I wish I could take as much sunlight from the report as can the Minister of Railways-earnestly I wish I could. I think I would have everything to gain if the result were as good as the Minister of Railways depicts it. I believe he is influenced by the best of motives in so presenting it; but I cannot see, that we can look forward to the future with quite the optimism that the Minister of Railways expresses.
He says that we lost in business some $17,000,000, and that this was atoned for to the extent of some $14,000,000 by economies in operation. I do not hold the National Railway Board responsible in the least degree for the loss of business; that is something for which other conditions are responsible altogether. The minister attributed those conditions to the comparatively small crop in western Canada. Our crop was something below the average, it is true, but the reduction in tonnage which resulted therefrom was only 2,300,000 tons, while total reduction in all tonnage on both systems in Canada was between 9.000.000 and 10,000.000 tons, if not over 10 000,000 tons-it was 8,800,000 I think at the end of October. Now why the difference? Is it due to the relatively small crop in western Canada? We had a large crop in eastern Canada, the largest in our history, and while the western crop was somewhat below the average, the farmer Obtained more for it for the purpose of his purchases than he had ever obtained since the days of the war. He was in a better position to buy in so far as crop returns were concerned. Why is it that the other tonnage fell off from three to four times as much as the grain crop? It certainly is not due to the National Railway Board, but I fancy if the minister in the quiet of his closet would ask Sir Henry Thornton why it was, he would find Sir Henry Thornton's explanation pretty much the same as mine; and if he would ask Sir Henry Thornton what the cure should be, I think he would get a remedy not very radically different from my own. The other business of Canada was depleted in masses, and
it was depleted from the year 1923 when we undoubtedly had no boom. It was not like 1923 in the United States when they reached the Mount Everest, when they bad a tidal wave of prosperity from which you would naturally expect some recession in the following year. No, we were in a period of comparative langour in 1923. But in 1924 we had iron tonnages drop off 57 per cent, and other tonnages drop off in lesser percentages; but down and down they went until the National railways lost some $17,000,000, and the employees of the National railways had to pay the bill. Those employees were out of work, thousands of them as compared with the year before. In that year $7,690,000 less went into their pockets because they were walking the streets. So we cannot take very great comfort from the fact that millions were "saved" out of the pockets of the workmen. And even this kind of "saving" atoned only in part, for the loss in tonnage of $17,000,000.
What, though, is the final result? We are $3,186,000 worse off on operation than the year before. The year before was better than the previous year. That was the first year of the new board; but the improvement was by no means as great as it was the previous year over 1921, and still further was it from being as great as the $20,000,000 improvement of 1921 over 1920, The rate of improvement got less and less until the end of 1923, and then ceased altogether, and now we are, in operation alone, $3,186,000 worse off and in fixed charges some $4,400,000 more. So, for 1924 we are behind 1923 a total sum of $7619,820.
Where are we going to be this year? The year 1924 saw an addition to the capital debt, according to the minister's own figures-and the minister was very, very delicate in his touch on this subject-of $118,000,000; according to the reports of the company it is somewhat more, but not very substantially more. That $118,000,000, even if it is right, will take $5,000,000 more to pay the interest on it. So next year there must be an improvement in operation of $7,600,000 odd, plus $5,000,000 odd. All that has to be overtaken before we have a chance to move one single inch, one single dollar, towards the balancing of our railway budget. Is it likely to occur? If the process of reckless expenditure of last year goes on this year, it will not.
The serious feature of our whole National railway position is this: It is the continued multiplication of the capital charges of the road. The government of Canada under the statute is responsible for new capital charges.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
If, as is stated, and very responsibly stated -the minister will correct me if it is a rumour which is false-great new investments are being made in Montreal for some proposed terminals, or other purposes, investments running into hundreds-yes into millions-

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OP ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OP ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Well into hundreds of
thousands. If this is true and on the top of these other expenditures, all in a mad race for a limited traffic, then we are not on the road that leads to solvency of this National system. Think of $327,000,000 being added to the debt of that system in three years and three months. I know the debt was added to, and rapidly added to, up to the end of 1921; but we had to restore a dilapidated system; we had to restore one semi-dilapidated; and we had to restore one wholly dilapidated- S,000-odd of freight cars alone had to be built for the Grand Trunk and for the Canadian Northern railways; and we had to put the thousands of miles of road into good working shape. But even then the rate of increase would scarcely equal the rate now after all this upbuilding has been done. In 1922, the last year of Mr. Hanna's board, this expenditure ceased, and only $59,000,000 was added to the capital charges that year. But, with the new board coming in control, $116,000,000 went on the first year, $118,000,000 the year following, and $18,000,000 in the first three months of this year. And where is it going to end? According to the reports of the company the total is $312,000,000; according to the total which I have given the figure should be $327,000,000. There is $14,000,000-odd unaccounted for, and I should like very much to have an explanation of where that fourteen millions comes in. However, assuming that the minister's figures are correct and the report of the company is wrong, even then the rate of increase is appalling, and it must be checked or we cannot see an exit at all. And it must be remembered that this pace has been set in the face of a continually contracting business; been set in the face of a contracting business to such a degree that $17,000,000 is swept off the receipts in one year alone; and it is set in the face of the most obvious fact-that you cannot multiply by advertising, by publicity, by radio and all those features, you cannot multiply, you cannot add a tithe to the business of the country. All you can do is take it from another system; and we have had capital investments in large sums for no other purpose than to help get a larger share from the one system to the other. Is that good business for Canada?

Every hon. member knows to-day-at least every hon. member who is prepared to admit, and I think we all are, that the soundness of the Canadian Pacific Railway is vital to the soundness of Canadian finance in general -that we would only be cutting our own throats if we were to impair the essential financial .validity of that system, Now, assuming that- we do not need to go any further; and nobody wants to be generous to them, they have done pretty well and we are looking after ourselves not them'- assuming that, surely it is not policy to throw the money of this country in millions in a mad race not to get more business into Canada but to get into one system a share of business from the other; the people of Canada to pay for it all.

because the necessities of the company determine the level at which rates must be set. You can go down just so far but you cannot go farther without interfering with the essential soundness of the enterprise, and you do not know what is essential unless you know the condition of its finances.
Now, it has been stated that from these railways we have the best service in the world.
I think we have. I think the minister is wholly right when he says that the trouble is our service is too good. Our service to-day is beyond the competence of the people of this country. We to-day are travelling de luxe over this Dominion. I suppose this is one of the glorious fruits of "competition." As a matter of fact it is nothing but a slow process of financial suicide on our part. We are paying for all this, and necessarily so. But there must be some way found by which it shall be made to cease, and we are not going to find it by the path pursued in the last two years, the path of heaping upon our own heads a capitalization beyond our competence to sustain.
Now, the minister says also that we should be very grateful, because while there have been bankruptcies of railroad systems in other countries, including the United States, there have been none here. Well, I do not know that we could take very much satisfaction out of that; I do not think the remark is very appropriate. If the Dominion itself did not stand right under more than half the railway mileage of this country why, of course, there would be bankruptcy. But the fact of the matter is that in the United States of America, while it is true their rates are higher than ours-we do enjoy in my judgment the lowest rates in the world,-in the United States of America, while there have been isolated cases of failure in their two or three hundred systems, the fact of the matter is that on the Wall street market the securities of the American railways have been in an almost continual ascent during the year 1924. Those roads and the traffic conditions of that country have been such that the public has confidence in their being paying ventures. The index that I have just referred to shows that the people of the United States feel that trade conditions generally, upon which traffic conditions ultimately rest, are on a sound basis in that country, a basis that justifies the continuous rise on the part of railroad securities.
What I would suggest to the government is this: Take the action which should have been taken many months ago. Stop these continual capital additions to the cost of the
national system. We are now up, exclusive of the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial, to a billion and a half. With those added, and with interest, we are in the two billion class. That is about what we have invested in our system. If we add interest on what we have put into the Transcontinental railway and the Quebec bridge we are away beyond the two billion class. The investment in railroads in Canada is colossal. It is one of the causes of the difficulties which surround us now; and we certainly should not through these years, even for purposes of service and competition, have permitted any directorate to run into the tremendous figures which this directorate has run into in the last two years and a quarter.
On this question of amalgamation I make no comments on the hon. minister's remarks. Certainly this country does not like monopoly, and if there is any way of avoiding it let us avoid it. But we are getting nearer monopoly every year that we permit to continue this process, which has been going on for twenty-seven months and has resulted in the position we find ourselves in now.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OP ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I am sure we all listened with a great deal of pleasure yesterday afternoon while the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) made his statement to the House. It was illuminating, and he made his statement in such a way that it was interesting, easily listened to, and easily understood. I desire to express my 4 p.m. appreciation of a debate with a little touch of humour in it now and then. It makes things go on a little more pleasantly. I think perhaps the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) make rather a happy combination, because-taking their speeches in conjunction with each other -if the one is a little too optimistic, the other comes along and brings things down to their proper level.
In commenting this afternoon, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) spoke about the tax-free bonds, and said that it was all right to issue those bonds free of income tax. I know a great deal can be said in excuse of what was being done at that time. These bonds were bought by all classes of the people, though no doubt the great bulk of them were bought up by wealthy people and wealthy corporations. A great many small investors bought bonds at the time they were issued, but the trend of these securities as to ownership affords a pretty accurate gauge of how the common people have been prospering

C.NJi.-Minister's Statement
during the last year or two. Why is it that the bonds have now filtered away from the small investors into the hands of the large investing public? I could tell hon. members about people who bought bonds years ago and who have none now. I am simply making the statement; the House can judge of the truth of it. I think I am perfectly correct in saying that the majority of the tax-free victory bonds are not in the hands of the working people of this country to-day. However, that is past and gone, and there is no use wasting time over the matter.
The railway situation in Canada no doubt is a very serious one, we all realize that fact. But I hope it is not without some ray of brightness, and that in the future it is not going to be altogether hopeless. I have no fault to find with the arguments which have been advanced by the right hon. leader of the opposition. I think it is just as well that hon. members should know all the circumstances and look at the situation from the worst possible side that we can see. I have no doubt that the statement my right hon. friend made, that we are over $7,000,000 worse off this year than last year in the way of profits in the operation of the Canadian National Railways is correct. In regard to the traffic and the loss of business on these railways, there are several different ways of looking at it. I know the right hon. leader of the opposition immediately went along the old track when he began to tell us why the railways were losing business. It was the old story of the closed factories, people out of employment and all that sort of thing. I think there might be another explanation upon which I may say a few words at a later date.
In regard to the management of the Canadian National Railways, I think the people of Canada to-day as a whole, are pretty well satisfied with the management of Sir Henry Thornton. But there are perhaps other factors in which possibly some improvement could be made. I often wonder that we hear so little in this House about the 'board of management which is supposed to advise Sir Henry Thornton. I do not know exactly what their duties are. I suppose their duties are to act in an advisory capacity. While Sir Henry Thornton may be a great authority in the physical handling of railways, I do not know whether he is a financial wizard or not, or whether he is capable of handling the finances of the railway just in the best possible way. How is he advised? How is he guided in financing the railways? Is the board of management composed of men who 
are able to give excellent financial advice? I do not know. I am not in a position to go into a criticism of the financial management of the Canadian National Railways; but I apprehend, Mr. 'Speaker, that perhaps something could be done along that line. I desire to say in passing, that I am not acquainted with the personnel of the board of management. Hon. Edward Brown, of Winnipeg, I imagine, would be a good man in financial matters.
I understand the government is responsible for the capital expenditures on the Canadian National Railways in the final analysis. While we admit and believe that the only possible solution of the problem at the present time is to allow the freest opportunity to the president and the board to conduct the business of the railway, yet, when large capital expenditures are being made, I believe the government is held responsible. I am not just exactly in a position to criticize with any degree of accuracy what is being done in this way, but I agree with the right hon. leader of the opposition that this is not a time to make extensive capital investments unless they are absolutely needed for the successful management and equipment of the railway as a going concern; and I believe that the utmost economy should be practised along that line during a time when we are having such difficulties and such deficits as are occurring in the operation of the railway.
In reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway, I agree with all the hon. members who say that the prosperity of the Canadian Pacific is almost as important to this country as the prosperity of the Canadian National, and we are interested in both. The only trouble is that we have to pay the deficits of the Canadian National Railway, and consequently it comes a little closer home to us than the other railway, which is able to pay its way in the meantime. At the same time it would be a calamity to this country if anything were to happen to the financial standing of the Canadian Pacific Railway; and when we work and speak in the interests of the Canadian National it is not with any degree of hostility to the Canadian Pacific.
In reference to the services that are being rendered, I do not know if there is so very much to be said. They are important in some respects of course, but I do not know that there is very much difference between the first-class car on the railway to-day and a first-class car which has been used in the last twenty years. I think we have a more expensive style of travelling, where the greatest

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
improvements and great embellishments have been given to modern railway travelling. I know that the trains run on time very much better than they used to. They travel faster, and that costs more money and may have something to do with the increased expenditure. Speaking of the services, I would like to take some members back thirty or forty years-and that is a good long time in the history of the country-and speak for a minute about the service we used to get from the Canadian Pacific Railway in those years. I can remember that when I came to Canada as a young man and first came in touch with some of the Canadian Pacific Railway officials I concluded that the aristocracy of Canada was to be found among the servants in the employ of that railway at that time. This is long ago, and whatever I say can be in no way a reflection on any of the men who occupied positions with the railways at that time. But I remember the time when the ordinaiy man would approach a railway ticket office with misgivings; he would ask a question and wait a considerable time before the gentleman in charge found it convenient to look up. And when he did look up and the question was asked again he would turn over a number of leaves and after a while vouchsafe a curt answer. If you persevered long enough you might get what information you were after. I do not think I am exaggerating. But what is the case to-day with the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways? You get the very best attention, the most courteous treatment, and accurate advice, and no one can complain in any degree of the services rendered by the officers of either company. I do not know what has brought about the change but there is no doubt that a remarkable change has taken place in the services rendered by both companies to-day in comparison with the state of affairs that existed in the early years of our history.
As regards advertising, there is a good deal in what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has said; you cannot increase the railway traffic of a country by means of advertisements. But what the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) said was also true, that one railway could not afford to have the other draw away its business. Now this is one of those cases where a little real co-operation might prevent a good deal of unnecessary expenditure and eliminate the present duplication of services; there should be no working at cross-purposes nor unnecessary competition between these two great railway systems. Within recent days the word "co-operation" has been used a good 187
deal; co-operation is coming to be more desirable than competition to a very large extent in conducting the business of the country. Personally, I believe that something must be done to get rid of competition between these railways; there must be more co-operation in the interests not only of the people at large but, as well, of the railway companies themselves.
The question of amalgamating the two railway systems was discussed a few days ago, and after considerable thought I am inclined to the opinion that it would not be a very good idea. It may be possible at some time in the future; it may become a necessity some day. But when I look at the matter coolly and calmly it seems to me that it would not be very wise to have an amalgamation of the two systems, for I do not think it would be a good idea to have either railway monopolize the business of the country. I believe I mentioned that fact while the hon. member (Mr. Euler) was speaking the other day, when I pointed out that if the Canadian Pacific Railway operated all the railways in Canada we should have that monopoly of which the minister epoke yesterday. In my opinion, if any company owned all the railways in Canada it would simply mean that the country would be in its possession. Consequently I could not for one moment think of the Canadian Pacific Railway operating all the railways of Canada. On the other hand, if all the railways were to come into the possession of the Canadian National Railway Company, and owned by the people of the country, with all the faith I have in human nature, and in the light of all the knowledge I am gaining in these days in political affairs, I could not believe that it would be possible to keep the railways free from political manipulation in some way or other. This is the situation as I see it. It is a fine idea, and it looks splendid at first sight, to have all the railways of the country owned' by the Dominion and run in the interests of the people, not emctly for profit but for service, but it is Utopian, and we are not likely to see it materialized'. The only thing we can do is to see to it that the two systems are run as profitably and economically as they possibly can be in order to give the best service to the people.

DISCUSSION OP ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after the very
able and eloquent address of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and the equally eloquent addresses of the two leaders opposite (Mr. Meighen and Mr. Forke), it is hardly necessary for me to discuss in detail the general railway situation. There is, however, one phase which was only briefly touched on by the minister, and also alluded to by the leader of the opposition, and that is the increase

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
in the debt to the public by the National Railways during recent years.
As hon. members will recollect, in my observations on the budget I spoke as regards that increase, and at that time I made certain assertions and submitted certain figures, all of which are reproduced in the records of this House. In addition, I offered to submit to my right hon. friend who leads the opposition the statements I had so prepared. I made that offer, not with any idea of magnifying my knowledge of the subject then under discussion, nor with the object of directing attention to anything I might know of the railway situation, but simply for the purpose of enabling us, if possible, to arrive at the same conclusion and the same figures, so we could give the public the true and correct situation respecting the increase in the railway debt to the public. The right hon. leader of the opposition did not accept that offer; as a matter of fact he brought down his own figures when addressing the House on the budget. Those figures entirely disagreed with mine. At the time I asked certain questions, which my hon. friends of the Conservative party did not allow me to continue very fully, and finally my right hon. friend wound up with the admonition that I should be more careful and deliberate in my inquiry and show less determination to reinstate myself in the favour of the government. Well, Mr. Chairman, that was not my intention at all in giving those figures. My intention, I repeat, was in order to enable the public to understand just to what extent the railway debt to the public had increased during recent years. That is of the greatest importance, because that increase is reflected in the combined debt of the country, and it is impossible to arrive at the increase in the combined debt without properly arriving at what is the increase in the debt to the public on account of the National Railways.
In his speech on the budget the Prime Minister gave certain figures as regards the increase in the combined debt of the country during the last three years. He stated that that combined debt had increased to the extent of ninety-nine million dollars. His statement was correct in every respect. To some extent it was founded on the figures which I submitted previously in my address on the budget, showing what had been the increase in the railway debt to the public. Now, my right hon. friend who leads the opposition-and I am extremely sorry he is not in his seat this afternoon-while agreeing with certain conclusions which I then sub-187i
mitted to the House, disagreed with others I would remark that so far as he is concerned it is quite impossible for him to agree with one set of those conclusions without agreeing with the other set, because if one set was right the other was right also. However, Mr. Chairman, there are three points which I desire to take up to-day. I shall not be very long in discussing them, but I would like to be very clearly understood what these three particular points are I desire to establish. The first is this:
That t'he proceeds of the railway bond issues made during the fiscal years 1920, 1921 and 1922 were not all used for refunding, that the portion not so used was not all supplied out of cash from consolidated account, but that the surplus over from the bond issues less refunding from cash during this period was 150,884,485 which was not added to the combined debt of the country. In answer to this the leader of the opposition says that the proceeds of the bond issues, were used for refunding-and any part not so used was paid in cash for refunding-and hence there was no occasion to add any part of the bond issues at all to the public debt.
The second point which I desire to make is this: that during the period comprised in the fiscal years 1923, 1924 and 1925, that is to say, the three following fiscal years, the railway indebtedness to the public increased only to the extent of $102,122,196. In that respect I am not using the revised figures as submitted by the Prime Minister; I will use those later. I am using these figures for the purpose of making those I gave to the leader of the opposition in his speech on the budget agree with these I desire to give to-day. In answer to that assertion, the leader of the opposition states, that the railway indebtedness to the public from December 31, 1921, to March 31, 1925 increased to the extent of $176,796,490.
The third point I desire to make is this: that during the three fiscal years 1923, 1924 and 1925 the combined debt of the country, that is to say, the net consolidated debt plus the increase in the railway debt to the public -I am again using the figures without the revision submitted by the Prime Minister-increased to the extent of $111,473,508 and using the revised figures as submitted by the Piime Minister, during the same period the increase in the combined debt during those three years amounted to $99.000 000. In answer to this the leader of the opposition says that from December 31, 1921 to March 31, 1925, the combined debt increased $262,561,105.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
Now, these are the three points that I desire to discuss this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, and these are the three conclusions I desire to arrive at, conclusions which are denied by my right hon. friend who leads the opposition.

Now how do I arrive at each of these separate figures in each of these years? It is important to get this idea firmly fixed in one's mind before proceeding. This is how the increase is arrived at. No, that is additional to the railway debt to the public taking into consideration all guaranteed and not guaranteed securities. The claim made by the leader of the opposition was this: That refunding had taken place for the issues which had been put out. My claim was that the proceeds of those issues had not been all used for refunding, and that the part not used for refunding not paid out of the consolidated fund in cash had to be added to the combined debt of the country in exactly the same way as the Prime Minister in his address added all the guaranteed and unguaranteed securities, less the refunding from proceeds of bonds and less the refunding in cash.
Now, the next point I desire to make is this: I stated that during the fiscal years 1923, 1924 and 1925 the present government had increased the railway indebtedness to the public to the extent of $102,122,196. These are the old figures, without taking into consideration the revised figures given by the Prime Minister in his speech on the budget. Those were the figures used by the Prime Minister, less the revised figures which he subsequently obtained. The leader of the opposition states that those figures are not correct. That the debt to the public in so far as the railways are concerned increased not $102,000,000 and some odd thousand dollars but $176,796,490. How does he arrive at that? He takes the debt to the public of the Canadian Northern Railway on 31st December, 1921, the debt to the public of the Grand Trunk Pacific on the same day, and the debt of the Grand
Trunk to the public on the same day. He adds these three together and deducts them from the debt to the public of the Canadian National Railways on 31st December, 1924, plus $18,000,000 subsequently, issued. Now, hon. gentlemen will at once admit that in order to make any comparison between accounts of any description those accounts must synchronize-that is to say that all the liabilities which are in the later account compared with the former account must be included in the former account, that if you eliminate liabilities in the former account it is utterly impossible to get a comparison of any description. That being understood let me say that I hold in my hand the report of the Canadian National Railways for the railway year ending 31st December, 1924, being the railway report that my right hon. friend quoted from in arriving at his conclusion that there had been an increase of $176,796,490 in the railway debt to the public for the period from 31st December, 1921-31st March, 1925. I would ask hon. members to consider what is in that account. It can be seen at a glance. It is the long term indebtedness of the railway company, which includes the guaranteed debt,-the indebtedness guaranteed by the Dominion, certain indebtedness guaranteed by the provinces, and certain long term securities not guaranteed at all. In addition to that this account includes-and I would ask hon. members to mark this well-certain equipment securities and also certain securities of affiliated companies. Now the same situation must be viewed with the 1921 accounts. You have to take into consideration the long term debt, the equipment securities, and also the securities of the affiliated companies which are reproduced in this particular account, or in other words the balances unpaid which are reproduced in this particular 1924 account. I will call the attention of hon. members particularly to one security mentioned in this account:
Five per cent Canadian Northern income charge debenture stock, $24,137,846.08.
Now the leader of the opposition arrives at his figure of $176,796,490 in the following manner. He took the Grand Trunk Railway account of 31st December, 1921, as taken from the Grand Trunk Railway report of 1921, page 8:
Interest bearing obligations outstanding.. $371,042,194 Less Dominion government (as per page 13) loan and interest	 76,965,322
Balance to the public	 $294,064,872

Nothing could be simpler; the matter is perfectly clear. The only way the railway could increase its debt to the public was by borrowing; and if you take the sum total of borrowings, less the sum total of refundings from bonds, and less the sum total of refundings from cash, you will get at what is the correct figure. The third point I desire to make is one I emphasized when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) was speaking. I stated that the combined debt of the country, that is to say, the increase in the net consolidated debt and the increase in the railway debt to the public, had increased during the three fiscal years 1923, 1924 and 1925 to the extent of $111,473,508, less the revised figures as submitted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The leader of the opposition brought forward an entirely different set of figures; he said that the combined debt of the country had increased to the extent of $262,560,105. In that sum was included of course the $176,796,490, which is the increase he claimed in the railway indebtedness but which increase was really $102,122,198-unrevised figures. He claimed also that the increase from December 31, 1921, to March 31, 1922, had amounted to $64,625,860; and his claim in that respect was this, that the new government having taken over on December 29, 1921, was responsible for all expenditures and all increases in the debt after that particular date. All I can say in reply to that is that the idea is preposterous. W'ho ever heard of new directors coming into a company who cut off as sharp as possible everything that had gone before and started out at once making purely new expenditures? Why on December 31, 1921, when the present government took charge, there were countless contracts and countless obligations that had to be fulfilled, with which they had had absolutely nothing to do with the making of. The estimates which were prepared and brought forward and on which all these contracts were based were prepared and passed by the preceding administration and all had to be met. And more than that, a great deal of the income of the country for the fiscal year 1922, had been paid in by December 31, 1921, and that was all applied to that period. Certain portions of the interest due for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1922, but securing up to 31 December, 1921, had not come in at all. It is utterly impossible therefore to strike December 31, 1921, as the line of demarcation and to say that the debt at that particular period of the year was such and such an amount, and that at March 31, 1922, it had increased by reason of the operations of this government, in that particular period, to the extent of $64,625,000. The only fair way to take the increase in the debt, the only just and reasonable way, is to take the commencement of the fiscal year 1923, when the present government took charge and entered into their own obligations, plus the obligations of the preceding administration, for which they were responsible

C.NJt.-Minister's Statement
in great part and which they had to carry out. Further than that, my right hon. friend submitted certain other calculations which brought the increase, as he figures it, up to $262,000,000 odd. I have prepared, and with the permission of the House I shall place on Hansard, figures showing exactly what was the	increase	in	the	combined debt for	the two	3-year periodsin question-that	is to say,	for	the	3-yearperiod fiscal years 1920, 1921 and 1922 and for the 3-year period 1923, 1924 and 1925. And as I have stated, the increase in the net consolidated and in the railway debt to the public for the period fiscal years 1923, 1924, 1925, the figures in regard to which I have checked up, balancing them correctly in all respects, comes to a total of $111,473,508 which is the increase in the combined debt. Taking from that the adjustments given	by	the	Prime
Minister in his speech, as will be seen at page 2645 of Hansard, of $11,643,000, it makes the net increase in the combined debt for the 3-year period of fiscal years 1923, 1924 and 1925 inclusive the sum of $99,830,508.
These are the three points I desire to bring out, and I have submitted my authorities. These authorities and statements, as I have said, will be placed on Hansard to prove these
thiee points, which are these: That during the first 3-year period covering the fiscal years 1920, 1921 and 1922 the railway indebtedness to the public increased by over $50.000.000. which should have been added to the public debt and which was not so added; that during the succeeding 3-year period the railway indebtedness to the public increased $102,000,000, which was added to the combined debt of the country, and not by $176,000.000; and that the combined debt of the country increased during the last three fiscal years $99 830,508.

C.NJ{.-Minister's Statement

Mr. Chairman, I am not going into details of the financial statement which has been submitted by the hon. member for St. Lawrence^St. George (Mr. Marler). I know the debt of Canada to-day is enormous, a large amount of it being due to ithe war, and also to unnecessary expenditure in railroad building. Faced with that condition, we have to find a way to meet it and to reduce our expenses, if this is possible. The net result, I find, is that we are not meeting the situation, but we are continuing in the carnival of extravagance in connection with railways that was begun some years ago.
Not long ago in this House I took occasion to draw the attention of hon. members and of the country to this mad carnival of extravagance, and while I did not get much of a report in the newspapers, I got a fair report in Hansard. Somehow the discussion I then started has spread all over the country, and to-day there is one question, and one question only, before the public: How can this awful carnival of extravagance be stopped?-how can -curtailment be effected which will not injure the transportation service, and so help us to retrieve something from the mistakes that we have made in the past? My proposal was a very simple one, and it fitted in with the proposal made by the government to get control of ocean rates. I had the hardihood- perhaps it was courage-to suggest that the first thing to do in the way of solving this serious condition of railway extravagance was for the government to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which not only has a good railway system but also a first-class steamship service; and that if these two services were taken over and co-ordinated with the National, we would get a real steamship service which would enable us to control the ocean freight rates, and we could proceed- to solve the railway question, which continues to become more and more serious, and which will almost wreck the country if it is not solved. The ex-Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) to-day said that something must be done or wreck will come to somebody. I say this also, that that excellent railroad, referred to this afternoon by the leader of the opposition, the Canadian Pacific, will eventually be wrecked by the competition that is being forced on it by these demands for unnecessary railway services.
The Minister of Railways admitted practically everything said either by myself or by the member for North Waterloo as to the awful railway extravagance that prevails. The hon. member (Mr. Euler) made some in-188
quiries and was in touch with Sir Henry Thornton when he prepared his argument, in the course -of which he said, in effect, that if there was consolidation of these two railway systems, the economies that could be put into operation by reason of the consolidation would effect a saving to the country of $100,000,000 a year. That statement has not been denied. The public of C-anada who have to pay this debt and pay the railway charges will hold this parliament responsible -will hold this government, this official opposition, and gentlemen down the line in their capacity as a portion of the opposition responsible-if we do not try to cure this evil.
Now, the minister said that certain proposals -had been made to do away with this duplication, and also that certain proposals had been made in regard to a merger of the -two railway systems; but virtually he said that it could not quite be done, that nobody wished to stop the fine service that the Canadian Pacific is giving to the country, that that company 'had to bg kept in existence, and he -made other statements along that line. But the responsibility is on him to deal with this situation, and not to sidestep the issue-for I take it that what he said amounts to sidestepping. In referring to my proposal, or the proposal of the member for North Waterloo, the minister also said that there was not anything definite to be dealt with. Well, I want to tell hi-m -that on March 31 of this year, when I brought up this question, I did present to the House and to the country-and it will be found on page 1771 of Hansard-a definite proposal to stop this awful -extravagance, to secure economies, and so bring relief to the country. If anybody cares to turn up that he will find it all on that page. I have this further to say, that while I was brought up as a newspaper man and -had a paper at one time, -through which I could place my views before the public generally, not a newspaper in this country has published that little statement, which is a proposal to overcome this difficulty.
The main part of my proposal the Minister of Railways sidesteps again. My proposal was this-and he must deal with it, no matter what the cost of these railways was to us if we want to stop this carnival of extravagance, if we want to deal with the question effectively-we must consolidate the railways or we will get deeper and deeper into debt. It has been proposed that the two organizations should co-operate to cut off a train here and a train there. That

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

will give some relief, but the main relief can come only from consolidation. We must take the two systems and then by co-ordinating them we shall be able to give the best service at the smallest cost, and gradually pull the country out of the hole. But the government is not dealing with that proposal, nobody in this House is dealing with it. And yet the people are demanding that it be dealt with, and it will be the principal question before the electors when the next election is held. I am not going into the details of my proposal any further. The leader of the opposition in the course of his address here this afternoon justified the Canadian Pacific Railway, perhaps very properly so, and he seemed to think it was absolutely essential to the people of Canada that the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National be kept in this state of most extravagant competition. I say this duplication of services, wherever unnecessary, must cease, and the only way to bring about its cessation is to create public opinion in that direction, and I am confident that that public opinion is now being created and will enforce itself in such a way as to compel some action by parliament.
Let me relate a little experience I had last week in regard to this duplication of services. After the all-night session, having an engage-men in Toronto for that day, I had the alternative of taking a local train from here to Bediell and there connecting with the Canadian, the Canadian Pacific train which arrives from' Montreal that morning, and proceeding thence direct to Toronto; or I could go to Cobourg and' there transfer to the International, the old Grand Trunk train of the Canadian National. Well. I made that transfer, and what did I see? Before I got to Belleville I had reached the area of competition which is the most lamentable and most shameful thing before the Canadian people to-day. For two hours the trains of these two different lines, trains of the Montreal-Toronto route, were racing each other to see which would get to Toronto first, and they were not as far apart as half way across the floor of this House. There they were, two mad trains rushing to Toronto, neither overloaded with passengers; the passengers looking out the windows, admiring the race and joking about it, and wondering at whose expense it was kept up. That went on until there was a diversion, but the race continued with the trains some distance apart. Now, that kind of race is going on all over the country through the unnecessary duplication of main lines and also on the branch lines system. My hon. friends of the Pro-

gressive party say it must continue in regard to the west. Well, if it is to continue they will have to pay the cost, because the people of Canada will no longer submit to paying it. The Minister of Railways and the government and parliament must deal with this situation, otherwise the country will become bankrupt. The hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler) has just pointed out that the debt of Canada, both on account of railways and on account of consolidated debt, is steadily increasing. I do not want to be an alarmist, but something must be done. The minister is getting the figures ready with regard to the amounts owing by the various entities' of the Canadian National system. The leader of the opposition said yesterday there were several hundred companies, was it, involved in the old Grand Trunk-
More than a hundred in the two companies.

More than a
hundred, and no doubt the same kind of bookkeeping has to be kept on for some time yet to clear the thing up. But we shall not get relief until this extravagance of duplication Ts stopped, not until then will the country be able to regain its prosperity. The leader of the opposition said here to-day that something would have to be done, otherwise ruin would follow. With the duplication that prevails in the west, not only in the way of transcontinental lines, but in connection with branch lines, and with the constant demand for more branch lines all over the country, all involving a borrowing of additional capital, where is the thing to end? Who is to pay the debt, and what is to become of Canada? First of all, we should have a commission of about three men, trained actuaries, the best men we can get, to ascertain what the debt is in regard to the railways and what the debt is also of the country in connection with the war and other things; but I would clean up the railway question first. I would end all this discussion in parliament and the throwing of charges across the floor of the House as to what the actual amount of the indebtedness is. We know it is away up in the hundreds of millions; it is in the billions and it_ is growing, while the country is not growing proportionately to that increasing debt. I asked the minister about consolidation yesterday and he said it would take quite some time yet, perhaps two or three years. He is a very busy man, so I would get three of the best men available, put them in a room, give them the books and any clerical assistance they need, and have them get at the real

C.AT.R.-Minister's Statement
truth of our commitments in regard to these railways, as well as find out what are the essential railway services that ought to be maintained. As to the consolidation of the railways, I would suggest that once the two great systems are consolidated they should be put in charge of a board of from three to five men made up from t'he executives that now administer the two railways. The Canadian Pacific have succeeded in making good in connection with their railway, and they should certainly have representation on that commission. I would take care of the interests of the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific in a reasonable way; I would not want to see them wrecked. So we want one special commission to ascertain the debt and devise a scheme for paying it off, and we want equally a commission of from three to five men of recognized ability, men who have had successful experience in connection with the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, to make recommendations as to consolidation. I would say ito this new commission composed of the best men of the executives of the two railways:	Your duty
is to examine the railway services of Canada to-day, and find out what is the best way to reconstruct them, and most of all to re-route the traffic. I questioned the minister about that yesterday, and he said that he had some idea of it, but the real solution of the railway problem in Canada to-day is to re-route the services.

My hon. friend is
attributing to me so many things that I did not ^ say he has said at least a dozen things I did not say or even hint at-that I cannot be interrupting him all the time to contradict them. I just wanted to ask him, does the scheme he outlines now mean government ownership?

Absolutely. Government ownership has proven itself. It is the redeeming feature in the world to-day in connection with the problems of the world. I want to tell my hon. friend, and I have said it before in the House, that the greatest experiment in public ownership to-day is the National Reserve Bank system which is providing the reparations of the world in connection with the Great war. Public ownership in Canada has proven itself in the National Railways, and in Ontario, in the Hydro Electric system. We are running our street railways with electric power distributed under public ownership. I see the dangers of public ownership; I admit there are-some dangers. I see the danger of political interference, but political interference is nothing compared to 188|
this wild carnival of unnecessary overexpenditure in connection with the railways.
I have stated once before that there has to be a consolidation. I have gone further and I have said to-day that there has to be a consolidation of-the debt. I have gone still another step to-day, and I have said that a commission of three or five men made up of the members of the executive of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, with the Canadian National having a majority on that commission, should be appointed, and I would put on them the duty of giving the people a fair and reasonable service clear across the continent, but no unnecessary trains, no unnecessary extravagance, no expenditure in advertising, no expenditure in soliciting business, but simply provide a railway service that will do the business of the country and allow us to get out of debt, j see my friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) is listening to me now. He assisted -perhaps he did more than I did-I claim no special credit for it, but between us we have called the attention of the people of Canada to the condition of affairs that exists, and now that the people have been seized of it and want to see something effected we find the government saying that this mad dance must continue-choose your partners and on with the dance. I say, Mr. Speaker, this mad dance must stop, and that a cure must come. I have suggested the cure of ascertaining the debt, I have suggested the cure of consolidation, and I have also suggested to-day that a commission of operation be made up of the executive of the two systems which will find a way to reduce the expenditure, to improve the service, and to help us get on our feet again.
I absolutely disagree with the statement made by the leader of the Progressives that he wants to see the two systems kept in the west. It is all very good to have them if you can pay for them, but can we pay for this unnecessary duplication? I admit what has been stated in the House, that eventually immigration may come to our relief, and may call for more extensive services than we have to-day, but-

Is the hon. member
sure that he is quoting the leader of the Progressives accurately, that he insisted that the two systems must continue? I do not believe he is.

I took him to
mean that, and I am taking also what I read in the western papers.
C.NJt.-Minister's Statement

But you are quoting
the leader of the Progressives, not the western papers.
I said the leader of the opposition said to-day that he wants to see the Canadian Pacific remain where it is in competition with the Canadian National.

But that is not the
leader of the Progressives.
Who said that?

You are now quoting
the leader of the official opposition.

No, if I may mention the gentleman by name, I am referring to Mr. Forke. He practically said today that he wanted the two systems maintained, that they were essential to the development of the west. I say all that the west can call for, and all that this province and the east can call for, is a reasonable service based on consolidation of the two systems and the wiping out of all unnecessary trains and unnecessary equipment, and the adoption probably of the newer equipment that is coming, for to-day nearly everything in railroading is being scrapped. The new equipment will be an electric drive on the railways from electricity generated probably on the streams that run to the Hudson bay, and we have enough water-power on the slope that runs to the Hudson bay to give all the power we want to drive our railways. I may be asked, how would you get that power to our railways? Well, the scientists to-day are finding ways for the transmission of electricity under high tension; they are finding a way of transmitting it almost without wires, perhaps through a beam of some kind. They are working at something of that kind, and there will be a way of cutting down the expenses and improving the service, and of stopping this over-equipment that goes with this overcompetition. Look at the equipment of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National to-day! Half of it would give a better service than the two of them give to-day, and at half the cost, and with half the number of men. The world is crazy to-day for duplication. We meet it every day in every direction, and we have got to stop it. I have said that unnecessary duplication exists in this parliament. Unnecessary duplication seems to be the craze of the world; there is duplication, duplication everywhere.
Of speeches?
And of speeches. My hon. friend is a good duplicator, but I scorn the allegation.

I do not want to be
misunderstood. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member.

On behalf of the people of Canada I say, stop this railroad extravagance, find out what the debt is and consolidate it at the lowest possible valuation; then call in this commission from the two systems and put the responsibility on them of re-routing the service and of cutting off all unnecessary trains; let them give the country the service it wants, but no more than is necessary. For a time let us get down to the hard pan of the situation, and if we do that, you will see our country go ahead, and immigrants begin to come in here, and later they will be asking for increased railway accommodation. But in the meantime stop the extravagance, find out what the debt is, re-route the systems, and if you do that you will begin to solve the railway problem. But we are not solving it here when we talk about how big the debt is and how it is growing, unless we undertake the responsibility of trying to pay the debt and ascertaining what would be a fair valuation for the roads. If we will do these things we will give some real service to the country, and it would help us to recover from our mistakes of the past. In doing these things we will give some service to the country and we will try to retrieve our mistakes of the past, and certainly there has been a carnival of mistakes in connection with our railroads. If we do this, light will break on the present gloomy outlook, a great improvement will come to the country, and in that way there will be a better condition of affairs generally. Finally, we shall have a public prepared for economy instead of for a continuance of the wild extravagance that has prevailed in the past.

I do not know that I would have intervened in the present debate if it had not been for the gentle reprimand given to me yesterday by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). I should like to say, however, in regard to the question of immigration-which he dealt with yesterday and concerning which I asked him a couple of questions-that in my judgment there is no member here who is opposed to immigration. I think every hon. member recognizes that Canada needs population, that our railways need population, and that other things being equal we would be very much better off if we had fifty millions of people in this country. Every one of us wants to see Canada grow-wants to see agriculture grow, manufacturing grow, and indeed

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
all our industries grow; wants to see a very much larger, happier, and more prosperous population in this country. There is no difference of opinion in regard to that matter at all. The difference of opinion arises wholly in respect to the policy of assisted immigration-if you like, forced immigration, immigration regardless of conditions existing in this country.
Now, as I see it, Mr. Chairman, we have a situation something like this:	We are trying
to pour water into a leaky pail. We are using tremendous efforts to fill the pail, and the water is running out as fast as we can put it in. I brought to the attention of the House a year or two ago statistics in regard to our immigration policy for the last twenty-five years. I stated the amount of money we had spent during that time in connection with our Immigration department; and the results-the negative or absent results-were also indicated. Now then, is it sensible to keep on pouring water into a leaky pail? I want to stop the leaks, I want to divert some of our attention and some of our money to the stopping of the leaks. I only wish the Minister of Railways was in his seat; I would like to tell him, and tell the House, that if we would put more effort into the stopping of the leaks it would be to better purpose than simply to continue pouring water into a leaky pail.
Now let me specify one or two examples to the government. A number of us in this quarter of the chamber who are sceptical of the benefits to be received from an aggressive immigration policy under present conditions, are very anxious that the government should undertake some worth-while rural credit scheme. But year after year the government declines to act; we cannot get action. I do not know whether we can push it into action this year; we certainly pushed as much as we could last year although without much result. This is something worth while, this is something that will stop one of the leaks in our pail. If we can introduce and establish in this country a rural credit system comparable to the system operating in the United States we shall at least put some of our farmers in this country on a basis equal to that on which the United States agriculturist works. In that way and to that extent we shall equalize conditions as between the two countries. This is one way in which we may stop the leak in the pail and help to retain the population that we have. I do not think there is any use in getting foreigners into this country if they go out as fast as we get them, or if our native population goes out. I agree with the
hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) that the best immigrants we get in this country are those who come by way of the cradle-they are the native born and they are the people that are going out. And why are they going out? The pail is leaking, and we have not made a real effort, not a determined and sustained effort, to stop the leaks. My theory and conviction is that the sensible policy is to get at the leaks first and then we can easily fill the pail. Now I suggest that rural credit legislation would be one way of stopping the leak. A sensible and just system of taxation wou'd be another way of stopping the leak. But we cannot get the government to move in this direction either. I submit arguments and suggestions to the government in respect to the question of taxation. I tell them that the present system of taxation is onerous and unfair to industry, and a burden on the workers in this country; that it is driving the people out of Canada, that it is a bad leak in the pail, and I want them to stop the leak. But they do not move.
I have just mentioned two examples. Here is another example that has been already mentioned by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), namely, the amalgamation of ' our two great railway systems. It has been pointed" out, and I do not think it has been denied, that thus we can stop a leak to the extent of $100,000,000 a year. That would be worth while surely. Surely that would help to retain our population, and to make immigration expenditures profitable, at all events to prevent their being entirely futile as they are likely to be under present conditions and as they have been in years past.
I must associate myself most definitely with the hon. member who has just gpoken, and with the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), in my conviction that the only solution of our railway problem under existing conditions is amalgamation. Some time ago I was a little dubious, I suspended judgment in regard to what might be the proper policy, but to-day I begin to see, and I am coming more and more to the conviction, that this solution will have to come. If it has to come why not sooner rather than later? If we must deal with it some time why not tackle the problem now? Why go on wasting money? Why go on allowing the pail to leak? Why not stop the leak now? I must take issue with the remarks of my hon. friend the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) who fears that if we have government ownership-I prefer the expression "public own*r-

C.N.R.-Mmister's Statement
ship"-that if we have public ownership of all the railroads in Canada we shall have political interference and inefficiency. Why have we not got it now? I ask him and the House why it is, if we must have political interference and inefficiency in connection with public ownership of our railways, that we have not got it now? If the argument applies to the whole railway mileage it will apply to half the railway mileage, or a little more than half, that we are now operating under public ownership. I cannot agree with my hon. friend in his fear as to the consequences. I know that the problem of maintaining efficiency is a serious one in connection with all our business; but I see no reason in the world why in a matter of this kind, we cannot get just as faithful service under public ownership as we can under private ownership. I believe, and I honestly believe, that in the very few years that have elapsed since the present management took over the Canadian National Railway system we have developed a very marked degree of efficiency, a degree of efficiency that will compare very favourably indeed with that now obtaining in the Canadian Pacific organization. This is surely a direction in which we can stop one of the leaks, this is one of the ways in which our immigration policy may be made effective and not remain futile as it has been in the past. The Minister of Railways chided me yesterday-as he has chided other members in this quarter of the House-and hon. members opposite have often chided us, with having no faith in our country. I have faith in our country, I want to say that I resent the charge, I deny and repudiate the accusation of having no faith in Canada. Indeed I will say this: if by extending public ownership to cover all railway systems so that we can save $100,000,000 a year I think that I at least in advocating such a policy have more faith in the ability, the loyalty, and the public spirit of Canadians than has the Minister of Railways or my hon. friend the member for Brandon. I wonder if I might recall to the Minister of Railways the definition of faith which is given in the Good Book. Faith is there defined as "the evidence of things not seen" and "the substance of things hoped for."
Has the hon. gentleman not got it wrong?
No, I think that is correct.
Better take another look. I think you have quoted it wrongly.

I am satisfied that I am
correct.
" The substance of things hoped for " and " the evidence of things not seen."

We have not yet in our railway business realized the ideal of economy, the elimination of these tremendous wastes that have already been so well outlined by the hon. member for South York. What we have in our mind's eye is the evidence of things as yet unseen, and surely we have the substance of things hoped for in the picture portrayed by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken; faith is "the evidence of things not seen" and "the substance of things hoped for."
Wrong again.

Well here is a splendid example of where it can be fittingly applied, and I suggest that if the hon. Minister of Railways wants to practise faith, he should accept the suggestion already made and tackle the problem now; a problem which surely will have to be tackled in the very near future at all events. I am sorry he was not in his seat when I made my earlier remarks, but I commend them to his serious consideration when he has time to read Hansard. .

I am afraid my hon.
friend _ will have to revise his scriptural quotations. He is all right in the rest rf his literature but wrong in that.
Who is to be the judge? The Minister of Railways?
No, the book from which the hon. member purports to quote.
The Minister of Railways has read it more recently.

No, but perhaps I have
a better memory.
