Minister's Statement

the railway commission should have the last word any more than it has now, but a railway company should have the recommendation of the commission before appearing before parliament for a charter to build a railway through any section of this country. In that way we would avoid the expensive competition that is going on now in railway construction and railway operation. Take, for instance, the train service between here and Montreal. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) told us yesterday that the president of the Canadian Pacific said it would not be fair to ask his company to eliminate a train that is now paying, and that these trains were paying. That is quite true. And the minister is hoping to get the two presidents together in order to agree on the elimination of unnecessary services 1 It looks to me on the face of it as a hopeless proposition. Take the two trains between Montreal and Ottawa at 8.30 in the morning, and the two at 3.30 in the afternoon. Do you suppose that either president would agree to taking off one train at 8.30 or another at , 3.30? Not at all. They are both profitable trains at the present time; but that business would be almost doubly profitable if handled by one train. If the railway commission were empowered to deal with the matter they might order one of the 3.30 trains of one company running from Montreal to Ottawa, and the corresponding train of the other company running from here to Montreal to be taken off, and in that way eliminate duplication. I think the same principle might be applied to freight traffic. We have the railways, but we are getting too much service for the traffic that is to be moved; that seems to be our great difficulty. The trains should be adjusted to the traffic. If there is sufficient traffic for all the trains now running, well and good, but if not, the superfluous trains should be taken off. Otherwise we shall never overtake our railway deficits. I feel that the minister should follow the suggestion made last night and bring this matter before the railway commission as early as possible. I do not think there is anything to be gained by delay, and I think there would be much saved by inaugurating this policy at an early date.
Some hon. members opposite, many of them of the Progressive group, and some members on this side as well, I think, and some of the Conservative party, are talking of reducing the capital of the Canadian National Railways. Well, at first sight that would seem to be a very simple matter-you merely write off a certain amount of capital. But it is not quite so easy as that. For instance, there are twenty-five million dollars worth of Canadian 'Mr. Cahill.]
Northern railway income debentures and about thirty-five million dollars of Grand Trunk Pacific guaranteed bonds, sold on the basis of dividend payments as soon as the respective railways earn dividends on their capitalization. These two issues amount to about sixty million dollars, and on these the Canadian National Railway Company is not called upon to pay any dividend because it is not earning sufficient to pay dividends on the prior securities, that is, the loans of the Dominion government. If you wipe off these loans, and relieve the Canadian National Railways to that extent, as soon as earnings are more than sufficient to pay dividends on the existing securities the surplus will have to be applied to dividend payments on this sixty million dollars. So by the simple process of writing off the Canadian National debt to the Dominion government, you let the railway in for payment of interest on this sixty million dollars, without getting anything back on account of our loans.

Has the hon member considered the seriousness of asking the people of this country who are producing the tonnage for the Canadian National Railways to try to pay freight rates which would provide dividends on a capital that is in no sense reflected in the earning capacity of the road?

Does my hon. friend think
that anybody seriously considers that at-present as a basis of rate-making? If there was anything in my hon. friend's argument, would it not be better to say-the Dominion of Canada will reduce their interest charge to the National Railways from 5 to 2 per cent, or som ething of that kind ? Or if you want merely a mark to shoot at, why not say:	When you
earn fifty million dollars we will reduce the rate. But that has no bearing on rate-making whatever, and is not taken into account by the railway commission. The only objectionable feature about it is that you put before the management an impossible mark to reach if you ask them to overcome the interest on the deficits and on the huge capitalization. I do not think any person seriously hopes that we will ever reach the stage where the Canadian National Railways will be able to pay interest on the loans due to the government.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have just one other suggestion to make. I think there are at present four committees before which the heads of the railways must appear at call There is a committee of the other House, there is a committee on National Railways and Shipping, there is the Railway committee, and there is the Ocean Rates committee.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
The special committee which was appointed last year, and re-appointed this year, the committee on National Railways and Shipping, is to my mind the proper body to deal with National railway matters, but I think entirely too much time of the officials of the railway is taken up by that committee. That committee represents a meeting of the shareholders of the company, just as the shareholders of the Canadian- Pacific Railway company would meet. The officers prepare their report and submit it to the shareholders, and it is either approved or rejected. They do that in a day. It would be perhaps too much to ask the- members of parliament or the members of this committee to get through with all the business of the Canadian National in a day, but I think matters should be so arranged that the committee could sit continuously for two or three- days in order to go through the reports with regard to the railways. In this way you would save not only Sir Henry Thornton's time, but the time of perhaps twenty-five officials who have to come to these meetings. These men have to dlrop the work they are doing, come here and await the pleasure of the committee. The committee sits for two hours; perhaps some gentleman in the committee has a speech to make, and most of the time is taken up by that speech. Then the committee sav to the railway official, "We will call you tne day after to-morrow." But when that time comes some internal arrangement in parliament has disorganized that arrangement, and the committee says to the official who has again come to Ottawa for the purpose of the meeting, " We do not want you to-day, but we will want you the day after to-morrow or next week." I think the committee should sit continuously from the time it starts until the sittings are completed-morning, afternoon, and night if necessary-go that the work could1 be got through in two or three days, thus obviating the necessity of the officials coming back here at odd periods with resulting disorganization of the work of their offices, of their inspection trips and everything else for an indefinite period. I also think that the question of the proposed branch lines of the Canadian National might well be referred to that committee, because after all that is the committee that is investigating the operations of the railway for the past year and it would be in just as good a position to determine the necessity or otherwise of these lines as the other committee would be. However, that is only a suggestion which I think would enable the work to be carried out with greater expedition and with less loss of time to the officials
of the company, and consequently less financial loss to the people of Canada. But I think the first suggestion to put this thing in the hands of the railway commission and let them deal with it genera'ly would save this country as much money as amalgamation, and would be a very much better proposal for the people of Canada. It would be the best solution, at least for the time being, of the whole problem.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Railways on his very excellent statement on the affairs of the railway for the past year, and I also want to congratulate him on his good luck in having such a fine organization to carry on the work of the huge undertaking we have launched upon in the way of public ownership in this country. I think it is nothing short of marvellous that Sir Henry Thornton has been able to make the showing that he has in so short a time. There is no doubt that the service on the Canadian National has improved beyond the expectation of any man in this House in the last three years. As has well been said by many members of the House, there is only one way they can now make profits from or get traffic, and1 that is by taking it from the other road; and the more they take from them, the worse off they will be. Unless we can get something in the way of co-operation, we shall 'be in the position of building up one institution at the expense of the other, both of which the people of Canada must maintain out of their own pockets.

speakeroldname: Mr. MURRAY MacLAREN (St. John city and counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) has made a suggestion as to the sittings of committees, especially the committee on Railways; he has advised that a change be made in the method of holding the meetings of the committee, especially with a view to saving the time of the officials of the departments concerned. This reminds me of what I learned last year in Australia, namely, that in the case of several committees, committees which take considerable time, meetings were held during the parliamentary recess. Of course, the meetings were arranged to suit the convenience of members, particularly those who lived a long distance from the capital. In any case it seems to me that with the view of allowing members to attend the sessions of parliament and to interfere as little as possible with -the work of parliament itself, these committees or certain committees might do their work during the recess. I understand that the plan is found to be a satisfactory one.

Would my hon. friend let me explain why? The reason why the Canadian National Telegraph Company works with the Western Union is that the other company made a contract to give all its business to the Canadian Pacific Railways, and we would get no return telegraphic traffic in exchange for any despatches the Canadian National might send that way. On the other hand, the Western Union give us a large share of their business, and by using their line we get an income that we could not get by using the other line.

Now there is a peculiar position. The Canadian National Telegraphs cannot and does not send cablegrams over the British cable; it transmits them over an American cable, whiie the Canadian Pacific as a rule sends the cables over the American line, but on request will forward them by the Imperial cable, the British-owned line.

Mr. MaoLAREN: It is so stated in the despatch. I think the Minister of Railways was present.

-its traffic being distributed in Canada over the Canadian Pacific Railway telegraph lines.
Solely.

Graham, Canadian Minister of Railways and Canals, pointed out that the Canadian government was willing and anxious to do everything in its power to assist the Imperial cable, "but" he added, "it must not be forgotten that the Canadian National telegraphs are being operated as a business operation." -with the Imperial cable-

the minister does not get it.

-but you cannot expect the Canadian National to hand their messages over to the Imperial cable if the National gets no traffic in return. If they are to get traffic for the Imperial cable we should get something for our own National lines in exchange.

Hear, hear.

Now, Mr. Chairman, it

the government will persevere in securing connection by this means or by accomplishing it in some other way. I do not propose to say more than a few words on the subject of the National Bailways themselves. Eulogistic remarks have been made regarding the Canadian National Bail-

ways but I feel that I cannot concur in them; I dissent entirely from them. Why do I say this? I do not say it because I am opposed to government ownership. My sympathies lean towards government ownership and I do not criticize the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways on that ground. I think that the board of directors have failed in the task entrusted to them, first on account of the most obvious extravagance and unnecessary expenditure. If you consult the people of the Dominion at large you will not find three out of four who will not agree fully in the statement that the board are expending, especially at this time, absolutely beyond what is necessary and what is proper. That is one very brief criticism I have to make. I cannot concur in this acclaim of approval and applause for the board. I think it is a harmful thing to do. I think it should be brought home to the chairman of the board in the most forcible way that he is not consulting the interests and the pockets of the people of Canada.
Another point I desire to bring up is this. While the Canadian National Railways con-time to use Portland, Maine, and New London as two of their ports, and while they continue to export over these rails and through these ports to the detriment of our Canadian ports and rails, it is a bad policy for this country alone. It does not pay. It pays the chairman and the board to make a little higher financial showing, but it does not pay the country. The money is not being spent here, but is being spent in Portland, Maine, and in New London, and so on. It is a bad financial venture, I take it, for the country to do that. In addition to that, it is contrary to. the most solemn undertaking of parliament and contrary to the enactment of parliament that such a thing should go on, and therefore if the board continues to violate those enactments, it is the duty of the government to deal with the matter. Now I can assure the minister-and I know he takes a deep and kindly interest in the matter-that we will not have contentment and will not have satisfaction, in a large portion of the country, particularly in the Maritime portion of the country, while this trade going over our own rails is carried on in this manner, to the detriment of our own ports.

I
should like to say a word on this important question from an agriculturist's
point of view particularly. I realize that the railway problem of this country constitutes a national matter of the first importance; but before we make any move in the way of easing the burden of taxation in this respect, I think we should deliberate very carefully, so that we would not make another mistake which perhaps would land us in as bad a position as we have been in heretofore. We have two splendid systems of railway, I think as good as any in the whole world. They traverse territory which is ahead of anything in the world for productivity. I am not one of those who decry this country. I thoroughly believe in Canada and in our ability to meet every problem facing us today; but not just under present conditions. The only limit to production from an agricultural point of view, from one end of Canada to the other at the present time, is the tremendous cost of transporting the produce of the farms to the market; that is, in combination with the high cost of production and the wages-which it is necessary to pay in order to meet the high cost of living. Any move we now make must be with the one object in view, namely of obtaining cheap transportation for the heavy products such as wheat, cattle and so on, to the markets of the world, because these will be our chief exports for many years to come. The prosperity of this country will depend on the ease and the continuance of the transportation of these bulky commodities to the markets of the world.
I believe in amalgamation, and I am quite in accord with the view expressed by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), and some other hon. members in this House. The railways are a public utility, and must be publicly owned and managed in the interest of the public. I think it is unreasonable to expect that a public utility managed by a private concern will be run in the interests of the people at large. I believe in government ownership, and I am convinced that the time has come, because of the organization and concentration of capital, that public utilities must be owned and operated by the government That situation must be brought about in the interests of economic freedom and justice for all alike. I believe that all railways and all railway subsidiaries, such as express and telegraph services, should be taken over by the government and operated on behalf of the people. Private ownership of these public utilities has proved a dismal failure in the past in this country, from the viewpoint of the people. The present National Railways, when in private hands, was
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

quite as costly to the workers of this country as it is at present. Amalgamation under private control, would be even worse. The terrible cost of the National Railways, totalling perhaps a billion dollars, is hardly any more than the country has paid for the Canadian Pacific Railway up to date, if we reckon in everything. The land, the money grants and the completed lines handed over to that great corporation, with the tax exemptions, are hardly less than the amount the Canadian National stands the country to-day. But this situation can be overcome yet, even if we have to pay full value to bring the Canadian Pacific Railway under government control. At present the railway situation in Canada constitutes a menace, with half of it in private hands and the other half under government ownership. I think government ownership would be a reasonable thing for an intelligent people. The present situation constitutes a menace both to good government and service alike. We have witnessed the spectacle of this House and the Senate being divided on the matter of branch lines; and the government-owned system has already been put to a disadvantage and will continue at a disadvantage for all time to come if the railways are to remain as at present half publicly owned and1 half privately owned. By that statement I mean that the people's rights have really been sacrificed by their own representatives for the sake of the privately-owned concern. I could name instances of this, because of the delay in putting the branch lines bill through. The privately-owned concern, the Canadian Pacific Railway, has practically made, their extension on the grade of the Canadian National Railway. A serious menace to good government and efficient service alike confronts us and we have to look this matter squarely in the face. The present railway arrangement in this Dominion can never be satisfactory, for there is distrust among the people and intrigue in government circles, which is the natural outcome of a dual system such as we have. The present state of affairs is fraught with dissatisfaction to the people in every way from the standpoint of service, as well as being pregnant with intrigue and corruption in our public life. It was mainly through the influence of the railways that reciprocity with the United States was defeated in 1911; which shows what a hold and influence they have over the popular will of the country.
Looking at the matter from another standpoint, I believe that either the government system must become simply a subsidiary to the privately owned railways, as they desire, to further their schemes of profit and
[Mr. Evans. 1
aggrandizement through intrigue, or the privately owned system will be reduced perhaps to a stage of beggary comparable to that of the Grand Trunk Railway, when nothing will be left for us to do but to absorb the whole thing. The immediate problem of the government railways at the present time is to get them to pay their way. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has mentioned immigration as the one thing in sight to which we may turn for immediate relief. It seems to me that there is no basic industry to which we may look for relief in our financial distress except agriculture. With the exception of the fishing industry, the raw product of which enjoys no protection, agriculture is the only industry that pays its way; and it is doing so without any law-provided privilege. According to the owners of tariff-fed industries, all their finished products are of less value than the labour and material that enter into their makeup. If agriculture were freed from this incubus to-day it could in two or three years' time double its production ; it could double its products for export and by 1928 it would I think tax our railways with their present capacity to move our wheat and cat-tie, our butter, cheese and meat and other products to the markets of the world. High freight rates during the last few years have seriously reduced our export trade. High freight rates have been caused practically by high wages; high wages have been necessary to meet the high cost of living; and the high cost of living is due to protection or the legalized privilege of price-fixing. The high cost of production on the farms has seriously cramped development in all parts of the country and it is unreasonable to expect much improvement in the railways until agriculture is freed from the burden of trade prevention taxes as a fiscal policy.
During the Easter holidays I took a trip to some of my old haunts near Owen Sound and it was borne in upon me that all agricultural development had years ago been arrested. I noticed that the same old heaps of stone that were hastily thrown into the middle of the fields when they were cleared were still there, and no improvement had been made. As a matter of fact, there has been no improvement. on the farms of Canada for many years past, and it is disheartening to see the many vacant farm houses and abandoned homesteads which once were occupied by settlers hopeful of founding homes and families. Under present conditions immigration is simply useless and it is fraught with serious consequences by reason of the failures that are bound to ensue with the resulting

drift to the urban centres. I do not want to be misunderstood in this regard; I believe in immigration. But immigration is not the first thing to be attended to: the first thing is to create the conditions that will enable immigrants to make a living on the farms. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) said in his speech yesterday, at page 3029 of Hansard, that if the men who come to Canada and those who are already here will show even to an approximate degree the stamina of our fathers and our grandfathers there will be more work and more men working in the country. Let us see. Our fathers and grandfathers who settled in Ontario came here to establish homes, and they spent all that they had in the attempt. They underwent many hardships in the hope of better times ahead. But as the years went on and the farms became cleared, the farmers found that in the meantime the government had made a bargain with another class of settlers, who founded cities, and who arrogated to themselves a privilege obtained by Red Parlour methods and political intrigue -the right to lay heavy burdens on the farm settler. These burdens have got heavier and heavier as the years have gone, until they are becoming unbearable, so that instead of farm proprietorship increasing, the increase is taking place among the wage-earning class in the cities, an increase out of all proportion to the rest of the population. Our railways as a public utility have been the first to feel this. The want of production is to-day the one reason why our railways are not paying their way. Only the other day I received from the Ministerial Association of Toronto, that good city, a circular letter protesting against immigration and consequent unemployment. The problem is already one of serious proportions in our cities. Now, these are the conditions at present prevailing; our farms are vacant and our lands undeveloped.
The Minister of Railways has said-and I do not think he should have said it-that our young men are. Losing their stamina as compared with our fathers and grandfathers. I do not think he should have said that of the youth of Canada. I think it is shown to be wrong by the very willingness of our youth in late years to shoulder the burdens of war. I believe that, given a fighting chance to-day, the youth of Canada wiilll redeem the Dominion from this financial! crisis. I say again, I bdieve in immigration as well, but immigration is not the first step to be taken. If the Minister of Railways had applied his words to the war profiteer, to the tariff-fed owners of factories, and t,o the 'bounty-bloated steel
manufacturers, I think his words would have fitted much better.
There was, however, a very hopeful note struck throughout his .presentation of the railway situation, and I believe that during the last three years the Canadian National Railway Company from being la by-word of mismanagement has passed to a position where a feeling of pride is felt by all of us in the knowledge that to-day we have a railway system unexcelled for efficiency. Sir Henry Thornton undoubtedly is doing well in that way. But it is certain that the farming population will yet need further railway facilities to carry their surplus products if they are to be given a fighting chance with other industries. I believe this is the reason why our railways to-day are not making good,-production is being diminished on our farms; and I think the best thing the government can do is to find out how to .relieve the conditions that have brought about this diminution and so relieve of the .incubus of every other industry in the country that one basic industry which alone can pay its way-agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, in the first place
I wish the House to understand that I am not wedded to the theory of public ownership, notwithstanding Sir Adam Beck and hydro and all that, but I must confess that in regard to our railway situation we are faced with a condition not a theory. Ever since the union of the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk under government ownership I have maintained that it is not feasible to conduct two great railway systems in this country in competition one with the other if we wish to be fair to the privately owned company. I am not a recent convert to this idea, for last session I spoke upon this question in the following words:
Let us look for a moment at the railway situation. In my opinion it is anomalous and cannot continue. Tme two great transportation systems comprise about thirty-eight thousand miles or more of road, built at a capital expenditure of over two billion dollars, large stretches of both systems running through barren territory which does not contribute any local traffic. In the next twenty years, even allowing for natural growth and development, there will not be traffic enough to pay interest on this immense capitalization. Yet Sr Henry Thornton states that he expects in less than five year3 to meet all overhead charges on the Canadian National lines, and I think he will be able to do it. If so, it will have to be done at the expense of the Canadian Pacific's business. Let our people be honest with themselves. This is a question of business competition, and as our business men realize more and more that every dollar they pay into the national treasury to meet our railway deficit is that much more added to their freight bills when they ship their goods over the Canadian Pacific Railway, there can be but one result.

Further on I said:
It is soil-evident that the people of Canada will never permit the Canadian Pacific to absorb the National linos and thus form a huge monopoly which would own the political soul of this country, so the only alternative is for the government to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway, as iit Should have done long ago. I have nothing against the Canadian Pacific; I think it has been a splendid institution for this country and I would hate to see anything happen to it, but from the way things are shaping to-day I see nothing but ruin ahead, in time. _ Contrary to what a great many think, the majority of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is not held by Canadians in Canada; in fact, only about 20 per cent of the stock is held in this country, 23 per cent in the United States and the remainder in other countries, chiefly in Great Britain. However, that does not matter. As I say, we do not wish anything to happen to this great institution, and I am therefore strongly of the opinion that the government should take it over in connection with the Canadian National lines. If these two systems were amalgamated they could be operated much more economically and the ocuntry would obtain the advantage in the lower freight rates.
That, Mr. Chairman, was my view a year ago. Since then I have travelled out to the Pacific coast on a trip of observation, going out by way of the Canadian National! lines and returning by the Canadian Pacific, and I returned more convinced than ever that our railway situation is an impossible one. For that reason, as I say, I think the government would be well advised to carefully consider this situation. It would at once relieve them of two or three very difficult questions that are looming up to-day. One is the reduction of ocean freight rates by means of the Petersen contract. If the Canadian Pacific were taken over immediately, its fleet of 59 ocean and coastal ships would be available and ^ in conjunction with our own merchant marine boats we should be well equipped to control ocean rates. Another difficult question is the equalization of railway rates, which could also be settled in that way. Thus, they could save the country from fifty million to one hundred million dollars a year-fifty million is the lowest and one hundred million the highest estimate I have heard mentioned. I tell the government that the people will not long stand for a continuance of two great railway systems once they realize that by amalgamation huge savings can be made annually.
I wish the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to understand that my concluding suggestion is not to be taken as a joke. I believe $200,000 is to be spent upon the Hudson Bay railway this coming year.
